\
**Part - A:**
\
\
To determine the appropriate value for the seasonal lag term, S, in a SARIMA model, we need to consider the seasonal pattern in the data. In this case, we have monthly temperature data from January 2000 to December 2001 for Dallas, TX.
\
Looking at the data, we can observe a clear seasonal pattern with temperatures fluctuating throughout the year. The data exhibits a yearly cycle where temperatures rise during the summer months and fall during the winter months. **Therefore, the most appropriate value for the seasonal lag term, S, would be 12**.
\
Since the data is recorded monthly, a value of 12 corresponds to the annual seasonal cycle. Using S = 12 allows the SARIMA model to capture the yearly seasonality and make accurate predictions based on the pattern observed in the data.
\
\
**Part - B**:
\
```{r, warning= FALSE, message= FALSE, fig.align= 'center'}
# Load the required libraries
library(forecast)

data <- read.csv("MeanDallasTemps.csv")

# Convert the data to a time series object
ts_data <- ts(data$AvgTemp, start = c(2000, 1), frequency = 12)

# Initialize variables for best model selection
best_model <- NULL
best_aicc <- Inf

# Iterate over all combinations of parameters
for (p in 0:1) {
  for (d in 0:1) {
    for (q in 0:1) {
      for (P in 0:1) {
        for (D in 0:1) {
          for (Q in 0:1) {
            # Skip the four cases where P = 1, D = 0, Q = 1, and d = 0
            if (!(P == 1 & D == 0 & Q == 1 & d == 0)) {
              # Fit the SARIMA model
              model <- Arima(ts_data, order = c(p, d, q), 
                             seasonal = list(order = c(P, D, Q), period = 12), 
                             include.mean = FALSE)
              
              # Calculate AICc value
              aicc <- model$aicc
              
              # Check if current model has lower AICc value
              if (aicc < best_aicc) {
                best_aicc <- aicc
                best_model <- model
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

# Print the best model summary
summary(best_model)
```
\
From the above best model results, the estimated coefficients for the ARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1) model are as follows:
\
\
AR coefficient ($\phi$): The coefficient for the autoregressive term (AR1) is given as 0.7183.
\
MA coefficient ($\theta$): The coefficient for the moving average term (MA1) is given as -0.4535.
\
$\sigma$^2: This is the estimated variance of the error term, denoted as $\sigma$^2. The value is 10.29.
\
The AICc value is given as: 1282.26
\

**Part - C:**
\
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# load library
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(tidyverse)
library(astsa)
library(xts)
library(lubridate)

# Set constants
n <- 252 #length of time series
# n_train <- 150 #number of obs. for model fitting
p <- 1
d <- 0
q <- 1
P <- 0
D <- 1
Q <- 1
S < 12

data <- read.csv("MeanDallasTemps.csv")

# Extract the time series from column B
x <- ts(data$AvgTemp)
x_pred <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_pred[] <- 0
x_se <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_se[] <- 0

# Set the training window
for (i in 1:72){
  
  final <- 180 + i
  x_train <- window(x,
                    start = 1,
                    end = final)
  
  fit_train <- sarima(x_train,
                      p = p, 
                      d = d, 
                      q = q, 
                      P = P,
                      D = D,
                      Q = Q,
                      S = S,
                      no.constant = TRUE,
                      details = FALSE)
  
  fit_for <- sarima.for(x_train, 
                        n.ahead = 12, 
                        p = p, 
                        d = d, 
                        q = q, 
                        P = P,
                        D = D,
                        Q = Q,
                        S = S,
                        plot = F)
  if (i <=60){
    x_pred <- append(x_pred, fit_for$pred[12])
    x_se <- append(x_se, fit_for$se[12])
  }
}

data$predicted_values <- x_pred
data$pred_se <- x_se
data$predicted_values <- as.numeric(unlist(data$predicted_values))
data$pred_se <- as.numeric(unlist(data$pred_se))


# Plot data and forecasts
# Subset the data from January 2010 to December 2020
data$Month <- as.Date(data$Month)
observed_data <-
  subset(data,
         Month >= as.Date("2010-01-01") & Month <= as.Date("2020-12-31"))
predicted_data <- subset(data, Month >= as.Date("2016-01-01"))

# Create the plot
ggplot(subset_data, aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(data = observed_data,
            aes(x = Month,
                y = AvgTemp,
                color = "Observed"),
            size = 1) +
  geom_line(
    data = predicted_data,
    aes(x = Month,
        y = predicted_values,
        color = "Predicted"),
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = predicted_values - 1.96 * pred_se, 
        ymax = predicted_values + 1.96 *
          pred_se),
    alpha = 0.2,
    fill = "blue"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Average Temperature", 
       title = "Predicted Average Temperature with Confidence Bands") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "black", "Predicted" = "red"))


january_2018 <-
  subset(predicted_data, format(Month, "%Y-%m") == "2018-01")

# Retrieve the one-year-in-advance prediction for January 2018
one_year_ahead_prediction <- january_2018$predicted_values

# Retrieve the upper and lower bounds of the prediction interval
upper_bound <-
  january_2018$predicted_value + (1.96 * january_2018$pred_se)
lower_bound <-
  january_2018$predicted_value - (1.96 * january_2018$pred_se)

# Print the results
cat(
  "The one year ahead prediction of AvgTemp for January 2018:",
  january_2018$predicted_values,
  "\n"
)
cat("Upper bound of the 95% confidence interval:", upper_bound, "\n")
cat("Lower bound of the 95% confidence interval:", lower_bound, "\n")
```

```{r, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("plot_q3c.png")
```
\
```{r, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("data_q3c.png")
```

**Part - D:**
\
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(tidyverse)
library(astsa)
library(xts)
library(lubridate)

# Set constants
n <- 252 #length of time series
# n_train <- 150 #number of obs. for model fitting
p <- 3
d <- 1
q <- 1
k <- 3

data <- read.csv("MeanDallasTemps.csv")

# Extract the time series from column B
x <- ts(data$AvgTemp)
x_pred <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_pred[] <- 0
x_se <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_se[] <- 0

model <- arima(x, order = c(3,1,1))
aic <- model$aic
AICc <- aic - (n+2*k)/(n) + (n+k)/(n-k-2)

cat("The AICc Value for an ARIMA(3,1,1) fit to the entire aMDT data  is:", 
    AICc, "\n")
```

\
The ARIMA fitted model does not produce predictions that capture seasonal behavior. The model predictions from part C were quite close to the actual aMDT data and the trend lines were almost similar.
\
In this plot of part D however, the seasonal behavior is not captured as good as when the seasonal component was mentioned in the `sarima()` model. The confidence interval is too wide and that can be noticed in the output of the January 2018 prediction.
\

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

# n_train <- 150 #number of obs. for model fitting

d <- 1
q <- 0
k <- 3

data <- read.csv("MeanDallasTemps.csv")

# Extract the time series from column B
x <- ts(data$AvgTemp)
x_pred <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_pred[] <- 0
x_se <- vector("list", length = 192)
x_se[] <- 0

model <- arima(x, order = c(12,1,1))
aic <- model$aic
AICc1 <- aic - (n+2*k)/(n) + (n+k)/(n-k-2)

cat("The AICc Value for an ARIMA(12,1,0) fit to the entire aMDT data  is:", 
    AICc1, "\n")
```

This ARIMA(12,1,0) model seems to have close values between the prediction and the actual aMDT. This plot in part E is very comparable to the plot in Part C and the predicted values and CI seems to be also similar to part C.
\
When the AR component is set as 12, it seems to capture the seasonal behavior of the data as compared to the ARIMA(3,1,1) model.
